JSON: Name: osh_aw_intervention_evaluation Title: A randomized controlled, mixed-methods evaluation of combined participatory ergonomics, targeted training, wearable monitoring, and safety leadership interventions to improve occupational safety and labor productivity in ageing workforces Short Hypothesis: Workplaces that implement a combined intervention consisting of participatory ergonomics, tailored training for older workers, continuous wearable-based health/workload monitoring, and management safety leadership will show a larger reduction in occupational incident rates and a larger increase in per-worker productivity for employees aged 50+ over 12 months than workplaces that maintain standard OSH compliance. Related Work: Existing approaches to occupational safety for ageing workforces fall into four families: ergonomics/physical redesign, safety and leadership training, health promotion/medical surveillance, and technology-enabled aids (wearables, exoskeletons, AR). Ergonomic redesign and equipment automation have demonstrated reductions in physical strain but are often evaluated without productivity or aging-specific stratification. Leadership and training programs increase safety compliance but produce mixed productivity outcomes and are context-dependent. Health surveillance identifies risk but rarely ties interventions to operational metrics. Technology-assisted solutions can reduce load yet introduce new cognitive demands and rarely show durable field-level effects. Cross-cutting limitations across prior work include limited causal inference (few randomized designs), short follow-up, sparse integration of productivity metrics with safety outcomes, low representation of older workers in analyses, heterogeneous outcome definitions, and scarce evidence on combined multi-component interventions versus single-component implementations. Abstract: This study tests whether a multi-component workplace intervention combining participatory ergonomics, tailored training for older workers, continuous wearable-based health and workload monitoring, and management-level safety leadership training produces simultaneous improvements in occupational safety and per-worker productivity for employees aged 50+. We propose a randomized controlled, mixed-methods design across multiple industrial sites, with cluster randomization at the team or production-line level and 12-month follow-up. Primary outcomes are incident rate (recorded accidents and near-misses) and objective productivity (throughput per worker and cycle time). Secondary outcomes include absenteeism, presenteeism, work ability index, and physiological workload indicators from wearables. The main contribution is a causal, field-validated assessment of an integrative intervention package specifically targeted at ageing workforces, with statistical mediation analysis to quantify which components drive effects. Expected outcomes are measurable reductions in incident rates and simultaneous productivity gains relative to standard OSH compliance, enabling evidence-based guidance for age-inclusive OSH policy and practice. Experiments: Study design: cluster-randomized controlled trial with four arms (clusters = work teams/lines): A) control (standard OSH compliance), B) participatory ergonomics + tailored training, C) technology package (wearable monitoring + ergonomics aids such as exoskeletons/adjustable workstations) + standard training, D) combined (B + C + management safety leadership training). Sites and recruitment: 8 manufacturing/logistics companies; minimum 48 clusters (12 clusters per arm), target N ≈ 720 workers aged 50+ (≈15 workers per cluster). Duration: 3-month baseline, 12-month intervention, 3-month post-intervention follow-up. Data collection: administrative incident logs, near-miss reports, HR records (absenteeism, turnover), production system logs (throughput, cycle time, defect rates), wearable sensor streams (heart rate, posture, step count, time-in-task), quarterly questionnaires (Work Ability Index, WHO-HPQ presenteeism), and semi-structured interviews for process evaluation. Baselines: current company OSH practice; additional comparative baselines include single-component historical interventions where available. Evaluation metrics: primary: incident rate per 100 FTE-months (accidents + validated near-misses), throughput per worker per shift, average cycle time. Secondary: LTIFR, absenteeism days/worker-year, defect rate, work ability index score, physiological workload percentiles (e.g., 75th percentile heart rate reserve), adoption/compliance rates. Statistical analysis: intention-to-treat mixed-effects difference-in-differences models with random intercepts for cluster and worker, fixed effects for time and arm, covariates: age, tenure, job role, baseline performance; mediation analysis to estimate component-specific contributions; survival analysis for time-to-first-incident. Power: detect 20% relative reduction in incident rate and 5% relative increase in throughput (alpha=0.05, power=0.8) with specified cluster and worker counts. Ablation/comparison studies: (1) Compare arm B vs C to isolate human-centered vs tech-centered effects; (2) within D, sequentially disable wearable feedback or leadership training in subclusters to estimate marginal contributions (component ablation). Sensitivity and robustness: per-protocol analyses, adjustment for Hawthorne effects via pre-specified placebo clusters, and missing-data multiple imputation. Risk Factors and Limitations: Technical failure modes: wearable sensor noise, drift, or dropout leading to biased workload estimates; exoskeleton or equipment malfunctions reducing compliance. Data/evaluation biases: selection bias if participating firms or workers are non-representative; Hawthorne effect inflating short-term productivity or safety signals; reporting bias in incident/near-miss logs; survivorship bias from early retirements. Scalability/compute limits: continuous wearable data storage and processing across sites require scalable infrastructure and may constrain real-time feedback. Statistical risks: insufficient cluster count or intra-cluster correlation higher than assumed reducing power; confounding from concurrent operational changes (shift patterns, demand variability). Generalization limits: findings may not transfer across sectors with different task profiles, informal workplaces, or cultures; observed effects over 12 months may not persist long-term. Regulatory/privacy constraints: lawful processing of health-related wearable data may restrict data granularity or require anonymization that reduces analytic precision. Ethical risks: potential stigmatization of older workers if interventions are misperceived as targeting capability deficits.
